content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper identifies a potential issue with the use of Shapley values for explainable AI: despite its solid axiomatic foundations, the Shapley value behaves poorly when players are "redundant" - that is, perfect substitutes for each other. In particular, adding duplicates of a highly predictive feature causes the feature's importance to be split among the duplicates, making each of the copies appear to have little importance on their own. The authors propose two potential fixes: adding a "consistency" axiom, insisting that a reward division is changed in the natural way when a group of players are combined into a single super-player, which turns out to be incompatible with efficiency; or computing Shapley values after first grouping the players together (for example, by clustering the features of a dataset).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
In my mind, the main strength of the paper is how it questions the Shapley value's axiomatic foundations. Much of the work in this area leans on Shapley's characterization without thinking carefully about whether the four axioms are justified for their particular application. It's refreshing to see this paper, where the authors are focused on guaranteeing new, desirable properties, and have no issue discarding existing axioms if it's necessary.

That said, I think the paper is lacking clarity about what precise application these new axioms would support. The paper begins by presenting Shapley values as a common measure of feature importance, but then develops a new axiom to help with feature _selection_. This is problematic because consistency is a potentially appealing property for feature selection, but much less so for explainable AI in general. Further, it's unclear to me why Shapley-based methods are worth using over standard feature selection methods, such as forward selection. The paper would benefit from being more clear about the specific application and its importance.

Additionally, I think the three contributions are lacking in theoretical support or novelty:
1. (The "Vanishing Effect"): While Example 2 demonstrates a concrete example of the vanishing effect, Proposition 1 provides poor theoretical evidence of it. Specifically, the authors make the asymptotic conclusion that a feature's Shapley value will converge to 0 as the number of redundant features increases, but cannot conclude that duplicating a feature once will cause its Shapley value to decrease. As feature sets have finite sizes in practice, supporting this stronger conclusion would be valuable.
2. (Consistency axiom): In order to support a notion of consistency, the authors completely change the definition of a solution concept, allowing it to output 2^n values rather than n. I find this confusing, as it seems less useful as a measure of feature importance and potentially computationally intractable. This section also fails to engage with prior work on existing consistency axioms that the Shapley value does satisfy (e.g., [vdBFJ13]).
3. (Group Shapley values): The final contribution does not appear novel: the authors simply suppose that existing methods from prior work might work well, without resolving the question of how to group the features at all.

[vdBFJ13] https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s00355-011-0634-2.pdf
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
I have serious concerns about the quality and novelty of the work, which are described in the weaknesses above. 

Additionally, the paper needs significant work to improve its structure and clarity. The text is difficult to follow, often using formal notation without defining it or referring to related work with little context, and the structure is confusing, including a large amount of technical detail (and even an algorithm) in the introduction. The authors should think carefully about organizing the text to make it more clear.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I think this is a potentailly fruitful research direction, but I am voting to reject because the paper does not support its contributions with sufficient theoretical evidence.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper is motivated by a concern that the Shapley value, as applied to the attribution problem in machine learning, gives decreasing weight to features containing similar information to existing features.

It presents a consistency axiom that holds if a measure of feature importance is insensitive to the 'grouping' of features.  They prove that this axiom, in general environments, is inconsistent with Shapley's efficiency axiom (Theorem 1).  Dropping efficiency in favour of consistency yields existing measures (Remark 3).

Some computational experiments are then performed with the group Shapley value from Marichal et al. (2007).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strength**

The search for good measures of feature importance remains in its infancy.  Contributions to this literature are important.

*Weaknesses**

Overall, this paper feels rushed:

1. it is poorly motivated: it's not clear to me why features with similar informational content should not be measured as less important.
1. it is poorly written: even 'consistency' is mis-spelled at various points; it needs a proper proof-reader.
1. it does not place itself properly in the existing literature: there is an extensive axiomatic literature, particularly coming from pure game theory; I would be more confident in the authors' claim that their consistency axiom was novel if they displayed more familiarity with it.  Is their measure the same as Marichal et al's?  Given that Harris, Pymar and Rowat's 2022 ICLR paper used Boston as an example, it would be very easy to compare results on that.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity**

I did not find this clearly written: it needs proof-reading; it is often unpolished (e.g. p.2 presenting density functions before explaining their motivation; p.3's discussion of 'consistency' before giving the reader an intuition into it, repeated with linearity...)

**Quality**

I was not impressed.

**Novelty**

It is hard to understand whether this paper makes novel contributions.

**Reproducibility**

Not attempted.
content.summary_of_the_review: This feels rushed; it is unclear to me whether there is actually an idea here that can be polished, or whether the authors are still coming to grips with existing concerns about the Shapley value's performance when features are not independent.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper studies the problem of measuring the importance of features in leraning tasks. The vanishing effect in machine learning is introduced as an important motivation, under which previous approaches based on Shapley value would fail. Then the paper shows that the "robustness" against redundent features (defined by Consistency) and Efficiancy cannot be both obtained in general. Finally, an approach called GroupShapley is proposed to solve the delimma.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The observation of the vanishing effect in machine learning is important. Although maybe not the first one to point it out, the paper provide clear theoretical analysis for it.

Weaknesses:
1. The implementation of the GroupShapley design depends on the task of clustering features. In the sense of the motivation example, if one can cluster the redundent features (or the corelation between features) at the begining, there may not be much difference between Shapley and GroupShapley. If not, then it is hard to imagine GroupShaley can really solve the problem. 
2. The theoretical contribution is simple and straightforward.
3. The presentation of the paper should be improved. The destriptions and notations are not easy to follow. I think this may be because the actual connection between identifying important features and determining the players of games is too weak. I would rather suggest not relying on the game theoretical modeling. Also, the experiment part is quite strange, what is the meaning of it and what can we get from it?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper seems to be written in a rush, with poor presentation. The studied problem is novel, and the experiments is of high reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper studies an interesting problem with important motivation. However, the theoretical contribution is simple and the presentation is far from being ready for ICLR publication.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies using Shapley value as the criteria for feature selection in machine learning models. It analyzes why the previous axioms for Shapley value and treating a model as a coalition game $(N, v)$ with $N$ being the set of features are not appropriate in machine learning scenario. Based on this, it then proposes the axiom of "Consistency" and the corresponding Group-Shapley-value framework. Numeric experiments are also performed for the Group-Shapley value.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths
The observation of the inappropriateness in previous usage of Shapley values in feature selection of machine learning models is considered to be novel. Meanwhile, it also proposes novel fix, the "Consistency" axiom and Group Shapley value.

### Weaknesses
It will be better if some analysis in concrete models of how Group Shapley values is better can be provided.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
This paper is in general written in a clear way and the main contribution is novel.

### Questions
- How should we choose the characteristic function and how does it affect the quality of the resulting Group Shapley Values?
content.summary_of_the_review:
**Honestly, this paper goes beyond the scope of my expertise too much. Therefore, my review is more like an educated guess and it may even contain some elementary flaws.**

This paper examines why previous usage of Shapley values in machine learning models is in appropriate and proposes the new "Consistency" axiom. Later analysis also justifies why Group Shapley value is good in certain extent, but it will be better if an analysis on concrete models can be provided.

content.title: Who are playing the games?
content.TL;DR: We show that one cannot get "efficient" Shapley values without correctly identifying the players (features) , and propose a solution to this conundrum
content.abstract: The Shapley value has been widely used as the measures of feature importance of a predictive model, by treating a model as a cooperative game $(N, v)$. There have been many discussions on what the correct characteristic function $v$ should be, but almost all literature will take the player set $N$ as the set of features. While in classical cooperative game scenarios, players are obvious and well defined, it is not clear whether we should treat each feature individually as a player in machine learning. In fact, adding or deleting a feature, even a redundant one, will change every feature's Shapley value and its rank among all features in a non-intuitive way. To address this problem, we introduce a new axiom called ``Consistency", which characterizes the ``robustness" of computed Shapley-like values against different player set identifications, and is specific to machine learning setup. We show that while one can achieve Efficiency and Consistency in special cases, such as inessential games and 2-player games, they are contradictory to each other in general. This impossibility theorem signifies a conundrum of applying Shapley values in the feature selection process: The Shapley value is only axiomatically desirable if the players(features) are correctly identified, however, this prerequisite is exactly the purpose of the feature selection task. We then introduce the GroupShapley value to help address this dilemma, and as an additional bonus, GroupShapley valuess have a computational advantage over the classical Shapley values.
